# Rasters {background-color="black" background-image="media/contour.png" background-size="initial" background-position="right"}




## Rasters

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(sf)
library(terra)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyverse)
library(tidyterra)
library(fontawesome)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 22))
```

::: {style="text-align: center;"}
Rasters represent data distributed continuously across a spatial extent
:::

:::{.fragment}
#### Examples:

- Elevation (continuous)  
- Habitat Type (discrete)
- Precipitation (continuous)  
- Impervious Surfaces (discrete)  
:::



## What is the Structure of a Raster? {.smaller}

A Raster is simply a `matrix` of values with some additional decorations on it that allow it to have a spatial context.  

```{r}
values <- rpois(n = 36, lambda = 12)
values
```


:::{.fragment}
```{r}
x <- matrix(values, nrow = 6)
x
```
:::

## Spatial Designations {.smaller}

For each value in the `matrix`, when it is turned into a `raster` object: 

::: {.incremental}

- The `cell` (pixel) has a defined spatial extent (width, height, & origin).

- All the physical space represented by that cell has *exactly the same value*

- The *courseness* of the raster is question dependent:

  - 3x5 matrix for Continental US may not adequately capture elevation trends.
  
  - 1m<sup>2</sup> matrix for elevation may be *a bit* too big.

:::

## Matrix $\to$ Raster

```{r}
library(terra)
r <- rast(x)
r
```


## Plotting a Raster

```{r}
plot(r)
```





## Matrix $\to$ Raster {.smaller}
Notice that when I print it out, it does not show the data, but a summary of the data along with some key data about the contents, including:  

:::{.incremental}
- A class definition (`SpatRaster`)
- The size of the underlying data matrix (rows, columns, and layers),
- The resolution (e.g., the spatial extent of the sides of each pixel).  Since we have no CRS here, it is equal to $nrow(x)^{-1}$ and $ncol(x)^{-1}$.
- The extent (the bounding box) and again since we do not have a CRS defined it just goes from $0$ to $1$.
- The `coord. ref.` (missing)
- The source, either `memory` or the name of the file the values are read from.
:::



## Getting Values from a Raster

You can grab data from a `SpatRaster` just like a `matrix`, though the output shows you which `layer` the data are being pulled from ([foreshadowing]{style="color: #cccccc;"}).

```{r}
c(x[1, 2], r[1, 2])
```





## Common File Types {.smaller}

Format | Primary Use Case | Multi-band/3D+ Support | Cloud-Native Readiness
-------|------------------|------------------------|------------------------
GeoTIFF/COG | Orthoimagery, DEMs, land cover, satellite tiles | Multi-band 2D | Native (COG)
NetCDF/HDF5 | Climate, atmospheric, oceanographic data grids | Multidimensional ($x$,$y$,$z$,$t$) | Moderate (moving to Zarr) 
ERDAS Imagine (.img) | Desktop GIS workflows, local image analysis | Multi-band 2D | Low (file-based)


:::{.notes}
- **GeoTIFF (.tif, .tiff) / Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF (COG)**: The undisputed industry standard for distributing and analyzing 2D geospatial imagery, elevation models (DEMs), and derived analytical layers.
- **NetCSF (.nc) / HDF5 (.h5/.hdf)**: The dominant standard for multidimensional, spatiotemporal scientific grids (e.g., climate projections, oceanographic data, weather models, and multi-band atmospheric sensor feeds).
- **Esri Grid / ERDAS Imagine (.img)**: The most prevalent *legacy* propriatary format still seen in and enterprise desktop GIS uses.
- **BIL/ASC**: A universal plain text format.
:::








## Loading A Raster - Example

```{r}
url <- "https://dyerlabteaching.github.io/CourseData/Spatial/alt_22.tif"
r <- rast(url)
r
```

Notice that this raster has *a defined CRS* and the extent is in the units of the datum (e.g., from -120 to -90 degrees longitude and 0 to 30 degrees latitude).


# Visualizing Rasters {background-color="black" background-image="media/contour.png" background-size="initial" background-position="right"}


## Built-in Plotting

Just like all things in `R`, `SpatRaster` objects can be visualized using built-in functions as well as functions from external libraries.

```{r}
plot(r, xlab = "Longitude", ylab = "Latitude")
```



## Raster Sizes {.smaller}

This particular raster is quite large (in terms of the number of cells)

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
r
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
These data only represent the elevation of the land.  Where there is water, the value in the underlying matrix is `NA`.  

Cell Type | Count 
----------|-------:
Land      | `r format( sum( !is.na( values(r) ) ), big.mark = "," )`  
Water     | `r format( sum( is.na( values(r) ) ), big.mark = "," )`

:::

::::




## Cropping

One of the first things to do is to crop the data down to represent the size and extent of our study area.  If we over 10 million missing data points (the ocean) and most of Mexico in this raster above but we are only working with sites in Baja California (Norte y Sur), we would do well to excise (or crop) the raster to only include the area we are interested in working with.  


## Cropping Workflow:  

1. Define a bounding box (the spatial extent of the region of interest)  
2. Expand it a bit so that points are not **on the edges** of the box.
3. Create an extent with `ext()`
4. Crop the original matrix to represent the boundaries defined in the extent


## Cropping 1: Bounding Box {.smaller}

Let's use the beetle data from the [Spatial Points Lecture](https://dyerlabteaching.github.io/Spatial-Points/slides.html#/sampling-sites) as the data we will be working with.  

```{r}
library(sf)
library(tidyverse)
beetle_url <- "https://dyerlabteaching.github.io/CourseData/Spatial/AraptusDispersalBias.csv"

read_csv(beetle_url) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326) -> beetles

beetles |>
  st_bbox()
```

## Cropping 2: Expand the Bounding Box {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

### Option 1: Eyeball it!

```{r}
beetles |>
  st_bbox()
```

Maybe rounding it to:

```{r}
eyeball_bbox <- c(-116, -109, 22, 30)
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment}
### Option 2: Use Buffer

```{r}
#| message: false
beetles |>
  st_union() |>
  st_buffer(dist = 0.5) |>
  st_bbox()
```
:::
:::

::::



## Cropping 3:  Define the Extent

I'll just use the old `eyeball` test to make the numbers 'round'.

```{r}
baja_extent <- ext(eyeball_bbox)
baja_extent
```


## Cropping 4: Cropping

To crop the raster, we use the `crop()` function and it makes a new raster (and I can throw the old big one away).

```{r}
alt <- crop(r, baja_extent)
rm(r) # this deletes r from memory
alt
```


##

```{r}
plot(alt, xlab = "Longitude", ylab = "Latitude")
plot(beetles, add = TRUE, col = "red", pch = 16, cex = 1.5)
```

::: aside
Notice the `add=TRUE` adds to the previous plot, and (2) Need to run whole chunk to see built-in plot overlays.
:::



## Cropping vs Masking

Masking is similar to cropping but with one main distinction.  When you mask a raster, you *do not* reduce the size of it, you only allocate missing data to the part you are not interested in working with.




## Plotting Rasters with `ggplot`

As you probably guessed, there is a `geom_raster()` available to us.  **However**, we need to convert the data from a `SpatRaster` (`matrix`) to a `data.frame` object that `ggplot` can read.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
alt |>
  as.data.frame(xy = TRUE) |>
  head()
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment}
```{r}
alt |>
  as.data.frame(xy = TRUE) |>
  class()
```
:::
:::

::::


## Converting A `SpatRaster` to a `data.frame` {.smaller}

`as.data.frame( xy = TRUE )` gives one row per (non-`NA`) cell with its coordinates.  I also use the `transmute()` function which does in-place renaming (rather than `mutate( X=y ) |> select( -y )`)

```{r}
alt |>
  as.data.frame(xy = TRUE) |>
  transmute(Longitude = x, Latitude = y, Elevation = alt_22) -> alt.df
head(alt.df)
```

## `geom_raster()` {.smaller}

```{r}
alt.df |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_raster(aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude, fill = Elevation)) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal() -> baja_elevation
baja_elevation
```

## A Shortcut: `tidyterra` {.smaller}

The `data.frame` route works, but it costs us a second copy of the data, hand-renamed columns, and remembering `coord_equal()`.  The `tidyterra` library bridges `terra` and the `tidyverse` so we can skip all that.

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(tidyterra)
```

:::{.incremental}
- `geom_spatraster()` plots a `SpatRaster` directly: no `as.data.frame()`, no extra copy, no `coord_equal()`.
- Uses the raster's CRS, so axes get proper °N / °W labels (just like `geom_sf()`).
- Large rasters are resampled for drawing (~500,000 cells) so plots stay fast.
- [Map-ready](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:WikiProject_Maps/Conventions/Topographic_mapss) color scales: `scale_fill_hypso_c()`, `scale_fill_whitebox_c()`, `scale_fill_wiki_c()`.
- `dplyr` verbs (`rename()`, `mutate()`, `filter()`, `select()`) work *on the raster* and return a raster.
:::


## `geom_spatraster()` {.smaller}

```{r}
ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = alt) +
  scale_fill_hypso_c(na.value = NA) +
  geom_sf(
    aes(size = MFRatio),
    data = beetles,
    color = "dodgerblue4",
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  labs(fill = "Elevation (m)")
```



## `dplyr` Verbs on Rasters {.smaller}

Without `tidyterra`: `names(alt) <- ...` to rename, indexing `values()` to subset.  With it, the `dplyr` verbs we already know work on the raster: each layer acts like a column and each cell like a row.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
alt |>
  rename(Elevation = alt_22) -> baja_elev
baja_elev
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment}
```{r}
baja_elev |>
  mutate(Feet = Elevation * 3.28084) -> baja_ft
baja_ft
```
:::
:::

::::


## Multiple Layers in 1 Raster

```{r}
plot(baja_ft)
```



## Getting Rasters with `geodata` {.smaller}

So far our raster came from a URL.  The `geodata` library downloads many *global* data sets directly into `SpatRaster` (or `SpatVector`) objects.

```{r}
library(geodata)
```

| Data | Functions |
|---|---|
| Current climate (WorldClim) | `worldclim_global()`, `worldclim_country()`, `worldclim_tile()` |
| Future climate (CMIP6) | `cmip6_world()`, `cmip6_tile()` |
| Elevation | `elevation_global()`, `elevation_30s()` |
| Land cover, soils, human footprint | `landcover()`, `soil_world()`, `footprint()` |
| Political boundaries (vector) | `gadm()` |


## The Bioclim Variables {.smaller}

[WorldClim 2.1](https://www.worldclim.org/data/bioclim.html) (Fick & Hijmans 2017): 19 *bioclimatic* variables derived from monthly temperature and precipitation (1970–2000 averages).  They capture annual trends, seasonality, and extremes, which is why they are a staple of species distribution modeling.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Temperature (°C)**

- BIO1 Annual Mean Temperature
- BIO2 Mean Diurnal Range
- BIO3 Isothermality (BIO2/BIO7 ×100)
- BIO4 Temperature Seasonality (SD ×100)
- BIO5 Max Temp of Warmest Month
- BIO6 Min Temp of Coldest Month
- BIO7 Temperature Annual Range
- BIO8 Mean Temp of Wettest Quarter
- BIO9 Mean Temp of Driest Quarter
- BIO10 Mean Temp of Warmest Quarter
- BIO11 Mean Temp of Coldest Quarter
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Precipitation (mm)**

- BIO12 Annual Precipitation
- BIO13 Precip of Wettest Month
- BIO14 Precip of Driest Month
- BIO15 Precip Seasonality (CV)
- BIO16 Precip of Wettest Quarter
- BIO17 Precip of Driest Quarter
- BIO18 Precip of Warmest Quarter
- BIO19 Precip of Coldest Quarter
:::

::::


## Downloading a 30 arc-second Tile {.smaller}

30 arc-seconds is 1/120° (about 1km).  At that resolution the world comes in 30° × 30° tiles: give any longitude and latitude inside the tile you want.

```{r}
bio <- worldclim_tile(var = "bio", lon = -112, lat = 26, path = "cache")
bio
```

::: aside
The tile is 126 MB.  `geodata` only downloads it if it is not already in `path`; on your machine use a `data/` folder in your project.
:::


## Bioclim for Baja {.smaller}

Same tile, same grid as `alt_22`, so the same `baja_extent` crops it.  `select()` picks layers by name.

```{r}
bio |>
  crop(baja_extent) |>
  select(bio_1, bio_12) -> baja_bio
plot(baja_bio)
```

## Reprojecting Rasters

Just like points, we can reproject the entire raster using the `project()` function.  Here I am going to project the raster into UTM Zone 12N, a common projection for this part of [Mexico from epsg.io](https://epsg.io/6367).

The `terra` library understands EPSG codes, so all we need is the code for that projection.

```{r}
new.proj <- "EPSG:6367"
```

## Visualizing {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
alt.utm <- project(alt, new.proj)
alt.utm
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
plot(alt.utm, xlab = "Easting", ylab = "Northing")
```
:::

::::


## Mixing Projections: The Problem {.smaller}

The raster is now in UTM (EPSG:6367, meters) but the beetles are still lon/lat (EPSG:4326, degrees).

:::: {.columns}

::: {.incremental}

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
plot(alt.utm)
plot(
  st_geometry(beetles),
  add = TRUE,
  col = "red",
  pch = 16
)
```

Base `plot( add=TRUE )` **does not work**: (-113, 27) is drawn at 27 m north, off the map.  No error, no warning.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
plot(alt.utm)
beetles |>
  st_transform(crs = 6367) |>
  st_geometry() |>
  plot(
    add = TRUE,
    col = "red",
    pch = 16
  )
```

You must reproject the points *manually* with `st_transform()` first.
:::

:::

::::


## Mixing Projections with `ggplot` {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.callout-note title="Automatic alignment"}
`ggplot` reprojects every layer that knows its CRS (`geom_sf()`, `geom_spatraster()`) on the fly to match the first one. No `st_transform()` needed.
:::

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = alt.utm) +
  geom_sf(data = beetles, color = "red") +
  scale_fill_hypso_c(na.value = NA)
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = alt.utm) +
  geom_sf(data = beetles, color = "red") +
  scale_fill_hypso_c(na.value = NA) +
  labs(fill = "Elevation (m)")
```
:::

::::

## Research Question 1 - Elevation Envelope

::: {.column width="50%"}
![*Araptus attenuatus*](media/arapat.jpg)
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- What is the elevation *niche* envelope for this species?

- Is there any indication that elevation is related to sex-bias?

::::


## Extracting Raster Data {.smaller}

`extract()` takes *all* the sites at once (as a `SpatVector`) and returns one row per site, in order.  `ID = FALSE` drops the point-number column.

```{r}
site_elev <- terra::extract(baja_elev, vect(beetles), ID = FALSE)

beetles |>
  mutate(Elevation = site_elev$Elevation) -> beetles

beetles |>
  select(Site, MFRatio, Elevation) |>
  head()
```


## Visualizing Elevation Envelope {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
The sites span `r min(beetles$Elevation)`m to `r max(beetles$Elevation)`m, but is that a *subset* of the landscape?

```{r}
#| eval: false
baja_elev |>
  as.data.frame() -> landscape

ggplot() +
  geom_density(
    aes(x = Elevation, fill = "Landscape"),
    data = landscape,
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_density(
    aes(x = Elevation, fill = "Beetle Sites"),
    data = beetles,
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_rug(aes(x = Elevation), data = beetles) +
  labs(fill = NULL)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
baja_elev |>
  as.data.frame() -> landscape

ggplot() +
  geom_density(
    aes(x = Elevation, fill = "Landscape"),
    data = landscape,
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_density(
    aes(x = Elevation, fill = "Beetle Sites"),
    data = beetles,
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_rug(aes(x = Elevation), data = beetles) +
  labs(fill = NULL, y = "Density") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

`r round(100 * mean(landscape$Elevation > max(beetles$Elevation)))`% of the land is above the highest site.
:::

::::


## Testing for `MFRatio` and Elevation Relationship {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
beetles |>
  ggplot(aes(Elevation, MFRatio)) +
  geom_point(size = 3)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
fit <- cor.test(beetles$MFRatio, beetles$Elevation)
fit
```
:::

::::

No evidence of a relationship ($\rho =$ `r format(fit$estimate, digits = 2)`, $P =$ `r format(fit$p.value, digits = 2)`).


## Research Question 2 - Elevation Transect

`const` is on the Pacific-side plain; `169` is on the Gulf coast.  The Sierra de la Giganta is in between.

> Does the terrain between `const` and `169` rise above the beetle's elevation envelope (`r max(beetles$Elevation)`m), and for how far?

:::{.incremental}
1. Connect the two sites with a line (the *transect*).
2. Put evenly spaced points along the line.
3. Extract elevation at each point & its distance from the start.
4. Plot elevation vs. distance.
:::


## Building the Transect 

Order matters (the profile starts at the first site), so make it explicit with a `factor`.

```{r}
beetles |>
  filter(Site %in% c("const", "169")) |>
  arrange(desc(Site)) -> ends
ends
```


## Building the Transect 

`st_union()` keeps the points in order; `st_cast()` turns them into a line.

```{r}
ends |>
  st_union() |>
  st_cast("LINESTRING") -> transect
transect
```




## Building the Transect


```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = baja_elev) +
  scale_fill_hypso_c(na.value = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = transect, color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_sf_label(aes(label = Site), data = ends, nudge_x = 0.3) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-113, -110), ylim = c(24, 27.5)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Elevation (m)")
```



## Sampling Along the Transect {.smaller}

A point every 500m needs *meters*, so project to UTM first.  Cells are just under 1km, so 500m steps skip none.

```{r}
transect |>
  st_transform(crs = 6367) |>
  st_line_sample(n = 100) |>
  st_cast("POINT") -> transect_pts
transect_pts
```

## Data for Plotting

Extract from the UTM raster (`alt.utm`) so the CRSs match; distance is measured from the first point.

```{r}
kmDistFromConst <- st_distance(transect_pts, transect_pts[1]) / 1000
class(kmDistFromConst)
head(kmDistFromConst)
```

## Data for Plotting

```{r}
elevationExtract <- terra::extract(alt.utm, vect(transect_pts), ID = FALSE)
class(elevationExtract)
head(elevationExtract)
```




## Put them into a `data.frame`

```{r}
data.frame(
  Distance = kmDistFromConst,
  Elevation = elevationExtract$alt_22
) -> profile
head(profile, 3)
```

## The Elevation Profile {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="40%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
profile |>
  ggplot(aes(Distance, Elevation)) +
  geom_area(fill = "tan", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = max(beetles$Elevation),
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "red"
  ) +
  labs(x = "Distance from const (km)")
```

&nbsp;

About `r sum(profile$Elevation > max(beetles$Elevation)) * 0.5`km of the direct route is above every sampled beetle site (peak: `r round(max(profile$Elevation))`m).
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}

profile |>
  ggplot(aes(Distance, Elevation)) +
  geom_area(fill = "tan", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = max(beetles$Elevation),
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "red"
  ) +
  labs(x = "Distance from const (km)")
```

## Research Question 3 - Connectivity in *Euphorbia lomelii*

:::: {.columns}


::: {.column width="50%"}
![*Euphorbia lomelii*](media/pedima.jpg)
:::


::: {.column width="50%"}
- Hummingbird Pollinated 

- Elevation-driven Flowering Phenology (+/- 100m synchrony)
:::

::::

How can we find the locations that share an elevational 'band' with any one target locale?


## Extracting Data From Rasters  {.smaller}

> What are the parts of Baja California that are within 100m of the elevation of site named *San Francisquito* (`sfran`)?  

To answer this, we have the following general outline of operations.

1. Find the coordinates of the site named `sfran`  
2. Extract the elevation from the `alt` raster that is within 100m (+/-) of that site.
3. Plot the whole baja data as a background  
4. Overlay all the locations within that elevation band.

To do this we will use both the `alt` and the `beetles` data objects.


## Isolating the Point

```{r}
beetles |>
  filter(Site == "sfran") -> sfran
sfran
```



## Extracting Data at a Point

To extract data from `SpatRaster` objects, we need to coerce (`sf` $\to$ `SpatVector` with `vect()`).

```{r}
alt |>
  terra::extract(vect(sfran))
```

&nbsp;

::: {.callout-warning title="Namespace Collisions"}
The function `extract()` is defined in the libraries `terra`, `tidyr`, `R.utils`, and `magrittr`, causing an issue for `R`.  It is not smart enough to know which to use, so the version in the *last* library that was pulled in will be used.  To *ensure* you have the correct one, you can use `package_name::function()` notation.
:::



## Filter the Raster based on Elevation Similarity

`filter()` the raster itself: cells outside the band become `NA` and the result is still a `SpatRaster`.

```{r}
baja_elev |>
  filter(Elevation >= 205, Elevation <= 405) -> elev_band

elev_band
```



## Make a *Background*.

The land underneath is for context (`fill = "gray80"`) and we omit the ocean (the non-`NA` cells) and convert this layer into a polygon (a `SpatVector`).

```{r}
baja_elev |>
  not.na() |>
  as.polygons() |>
  filter(Elevation == 1) -> land
land
```


##  Pulling It Together {.smaller}

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(ggrepel)
ggplot() +
  geom_spatvector(data = land, fill = "gray80", color = NA) +
  geom_spatraster(data = elev_band) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "darkolivegreen",
    mid = "yellow",
    high = "brown",
    midpoint = 305,
    na.value = NA
  ) +
  geom_sf(
    aes(size = MFRatio),
    alpha = 0.5,
    color = "dodgerblue3",
    data = beetles
  ) +
  geom_text_repel(
    aes(label = Site, geometry = geometry),
    data = beetles,
    stat = "sf_coordinates",
    size = 4,
    color = "dodgerblue4"
  )
```

## &nbsp; 

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(ggrepel)
ggplot() +
  geom_spatvector(data = land, fill = "gray80", color = NA) +
  geom_spatraster(data = elev_band) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "darkolivegreen",
    mid = "yellow",
    high = "darkolivegreen",
    midpoint = 305,
    na.value = NA
  ) +
  geom_sf(
    aes(size = MFRatio),
    alpha = 0.5,
    color = "dodgerblue3",
    data = beetles
  ) +
  geom_text_repel(
    aes(label = Site, geometry = geometry),
    data = beetles,
    stat = "sf_coordinates",
    size = 4,
    color = "dodgerblue4"
  ) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```
